claims.text: The starting material is AlCrFeNiSi high-entropy-alloy powder feedstock.
The proposed intervention is optimization of additive-manufacturing process parameters for AlCrFeNiSi.
The optimization includes controlling cooling rates.
Optimized additive manufacturing will reduce residual stress in AlCrFeNiSi.
Optimized additive manufacturing will reduce segregation in AlCrFeNiSi.
Controlled thermal gradients will minimize defect formation.
Reduced residual stress, segregation, and defects will improve the mechanical integrity of AlCrFeNiSi.
Optimized additive manufacturing will increase AlCrFeNiSi strength by 15% relative to conventional fabrication.
Optimized additive manufacturing will increase AlCrFeNiSi toughness by 20% relative to conventional fabrication.
Optimized additive manufacturing will improve AlCrFeNiSi wear resistance.
Optimized additive manufacturing will improve AlCrFeNiSi corrosion resistance.
Conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi is the comparison baseline.
The hypothesis is valid only within a controllable and optimizable range of additive-manufacturing parameters.
The process–property relationship may vary with the precise AlCrFeNiSi composition and additive-manufacturing technique.
A comparative experiment will measure strength, toughness, wear resistance, and corrosion resistance after optimized additive manufacturing and conventional fabrication.
The hypothesis is to be falsified if optimized additive manufacturing does not produce a statistically significant improvement of at least 10% in mechanical integrity.

contradictions.description: The prediction specifies 15% higher strength and 20% higher toughness, but the falsification rule accepts any significant improvement of at least 10% in an undefined aggregate called mechanical integrity. Thus, results such as a 10–14% strength increase or a 10–19% toughness increase would miss the stated predictions without falsifying the hypothesis under its rule.
